---
title: "Returns, Volatility & Fat Tails"
subtitle: "How big is a typical day — and how big are the strange ones?"
---



A **return** is a single number per day: roughly the percent the stock moved.
Most days are small; a few are wild.  This page measures both — the everyday
wobble (**volatility**) and the surprisingly frequent extremes (**fat tails**) —
straight from the basket.

---

## 1 · What a Return Looks Like

Here is one bank's daily return, day by day.  It hovers near zero with bursts of
turbulence — calm stretches punctuated by clusters of big moves.  The shaded
bands mark **high-volatility windows** (where the 21-day rolling standard
deviation is in its top fifth).

::: {#cell-fig-return-series .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r = R["JPM"]                               # daily log-returns, one number per day
σ_roll = r.rolling(21).std()               # σ(t): 21-day realised daily vol  (≈ 1 trading month)
hi = σ_roll > σ_roll.quantile(0.80)        # high-volatility days: σ(t) in its top fifth
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
ax.plot(r.index, r, color=COOL, lw=0.6)
ax.fill_between(r.index, r.min(), r.max(), where=hi.fillna(False),
                color=CRASH, alpha=0.12, label="high-volatility window")
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.7)
ax.set_ylabel("JPM daily log-return"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("Returns wobble — and the wobble clusters", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower left")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![JPM daily log-returns over nineteen years. Most days sit in a thin zero-centred band; volatility arrives in clusters (shaded), not evenly. The dense cluster in 2008–09 (the financial crisis) and the spike in 2020 (COVID) are the turbulent episodes the later pages name.](02-returns-and-volatility_files/figure-html/fig-return-series-output-1.png){#fig-return-series width=1064 height=489}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Volatility = the Size of the Wobble
**Volatility** is just the standard deviation of returns.  Quoted *annualised*
(daily std $\times \sqrt{252}$ trading days), it answers "how much does this name
typically swing in a year?"
:::

## 2 · From Returns to a Volatility Number

Volatility is not handed to us — we *build* it from the returns, in two small
steps.  First the **rolling realised vol**: slide a 21-day window (about one
trading month) along the return series and take the standard deviation inside
each window.  That gives a *daily* volatility series — its own object, one number
per day, that rises and falls as the market calms and panics.  Then we
**annualise** it: a daily std scales to a yearly one by $\times\sqrt{252}$ (the
trading days in a year), so the numbers read as "swing per year".

::: {#b61d8942 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r = R["JPM"]                               # daily log-returns
σ_daily = r.rolling(21).std()              # step 1: σ_daily(t) = 21-day realised daily vol
σ_annual = σ_daily * np.sqrt(252)          # step 2: σ_ann = σ_daily·√252   (252 trading days/yr)
print("JPM 21-day rolling vol — daily (raw) then annualised:")
print(σ_annual.dropna().head().round(3).to_string())
print(f"\ncalmest month: {σ_annual.min():.0%} · wildest month: {σ_annual.max():.0%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
JPM 21-day rolling vol — daily (raw) then annualised:
date
2007-02-02    0.133
2007-02-05    0.133
2007-02-06    0.127
2007-02-07    0.127
2007-02-08    0.128

calmest month: 7% · wildest month: 161%
```
:::
:::


The single annualised *bar* below is just this series **averaged over the whole
sample**.  Watching the intermediate series makes that obvious — and shows how
much it moves: JPM's quietest month sits near 10% annualised, its wildest (autumn
2008) blows past 150%.  A single bar hides all of that.

::: {#cell-fig-rolling-vol .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
ax.plot(σ_annual.index, σ_annual, color=COOL, lw=0.8)
ax.axhline(σ_annual.mean(), color=CRASH, lw=1.2, ls="--",
           label=f"whole-sample average ({σ_annual.mean():.0%})")
ax.set_ylabel("annualised rolling vol"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("Volatility is a moving series, not a single number", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![JPM's 21-day rolling volatility, annualised — the intermediate object behind the bar. It is calm (10–20%) for years at a stretch, then erupts: the financial crisis pushes realised vol past 150% in late 2008, and COVID spikes it again in 2020. The dashed line marks the whole-sample average, the single number the bar chart reports — clearly a poor summary of a series this lumpy.](02-returns-and-volatility_files/figure-html/fig-rolling-vol-output-1.png){#fig-rolling-vol width=1076 height=417}
:::

## 3 · Who Wobbles Most?

Collapse each name's rolling series to its average and you can rank the basket —
exactly as intuition predicts: banks swing hardest (the financial crisis is baked
into their numbers), with tech and energy next; defensive utilities and staples
are the calmest.

::: {#cell-fig-vol-bars .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta().set_index("ticker")
σ_ann_by_name = (R.std() * np.sqrt(252)).sort_values()    # σ_ann = σ_daily·√252  per name
colors = [CRASH if meta.loc[t, "sector"] == "Banks"
          else plotting.PALETTE["green"]
          if meta.loc[t, "sector"] in ("Utilities", "Staples")
          else COOL for t in σ_ann_by_name.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.0))
ax.barh(σ_ann_by_name.index, σ_ann_by_name.values, color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("annualised volatility"); ax.set_title(
    "Banks swing hardest; staples stay calm", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Annualised volatility by name. Banks (red) swing 35–50% a year — the 2008 crisis lives in those numbers; tech and energy (blue) sit near 27–31%; defensive staples and utilities (green) are the calmest at ~18–20%. The same ordering returns when we measure market beta.](02-returns-and-volatility_files/figure-html/fig-vol-bars-output-1.png){#fig-vol-bars width=1004 height=465}
:::

## 4 · The Tails Are Too Fat for a Bell Curve

If returns were Gaussian, days far from the average would essentially never
happen.  They happen all the time.  A **fat-tailed** distribution does two things
the bell curve doesn't — it is *more peaked in the middle* (more quiet days than
the bell expects) and it has *heavier extremes* (more violent ones).  The two
panels below show each in turn.

::: {#cell-fig-fat-tails .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
μ, σ = r.mean(), r.std()                    # fit r ~ 𝒩(μ, σ²) by moments
n_days = len(r)
z: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (r - μ) / σ     # z-score = (r − μ) / σ   (standardise to std devs)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.0))

# Left — the peak, on a plain linear axis, zoomed to the centre
grid: Float[Array, "n_grid"] = np.linspace(-0.06, 0.06, 400)
axL.hist(r, bins=200, density=True, color=BAND, alpha=0.85, label="JPM returns")
axL.plot(grid, norm.pdf(grid, μ, σ), color=INK, lw=2, label="fitted bell curve")  # 𝒩(μ, σ²) pdf
axL.set_xlim(-0.06, 0.06)
axL.set_xlabel("daily return"); axL.set_ylabel("density")
axL.set_title("The peak is taller than the bell", fontsize=11)
axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False); despine(axL)

# Right — the tails, as a quantile–quantile plot
theo: Float[Array, "n_days"] = norm.ppf((np.arange(1, n_days + 1) - 0.5) / n_days)  # Φ⁻¹ at plotting positions
axR.scatter(theo, np.sort(z), s=5, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axR.plot([-4, 4], [-4, 4], color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--",
         label="what a bell curve would give")
axR.set_xlim(-4, 4)
axR.set_xlabel("if returns were Gaussian (std devs)")
axR.set_ylabel("actual return (std devs)")
axR.set_title("The extremes peel away", fontsize=11)
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Left: JPM's return histogram (zoomed to the centre) against a fitted bell curve — the real peak is twice as tall, because calm days pile up more than a bell allows. Right: a quantile–quantile plot. If returns were Gaussian the dots would lie on the dashed line; instead they peel away at both ends — down past −9 std for the crash days, up past +9 std for the rallies. That peeling-away is the fat tail.](02-returns-and-volatility_files/figure-html/fig-fat-tails-output-1.png){#fig-fat-tails width=1185 height=465}
:::
:::


The right panel is the honest one, and the counts behind it are stark.  A bell
curve fitted to JPM expects about **13** days beyond 3 std in this 19-year sample;
there were **88**.  Beyond 4 std it expects **0.3** days; there were **48**.  JPM's
worst single day was a **−9.9 std** move — a Gaussian says a day that bad arrives
once in $10^{22}$ days, far longer than the universe has existed.  It happened once
in nineteen years.  **Excess kurtosis** is the one number that summarises this gap
(0 for a bell curve, **16.8** for JPM), and the heaviness varies a lot by name:

::: {#bb7b4e67 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# excess kurtosis κ = E[(r−μ)⁴]/σ⁴ − 3   (0 for a Gaussian; large ⇒ fat tails)
κ_by_name = R.apply(kurtosis).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("excess kurtosis (0 = Gaussian):")
print(κ_by_name.round(1).to_string())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
excess kurtosis (0 = Gaussian):
C       38.3
BAC     24.8
CVX     21.6
WFC     20.9
SO      19.4
JPM     16.8
GS      14.9
DUK     13.0
KO      11.4
XOM      9.8
PG       9.6
MSFT     8.8
GOOG     8.2
AAPL     7.0
```
:::
:::


Notice this is **not** the volatility ranking.  Citigroup (≈38) and Bank of
America (≈25) wear the crisis in their tails, as you'd expect — but Chevron and
Southern Co., an oil major and a utility, sit near the top too, fattened by a
handful of rare shocks (the 2020 oil-price war, isolated utility sell-offs).
Meanwhile Apple — the most volatile name *outside the banks* — has the thinnest
tails of all.
Kurtosis measures the rare shock, not the everyday wobble; a name can swing a lot
without ever doing anything truly strange, and a calm name can hide one violent day.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why Fat Tails Matter Later
A Gaussian model of returns *understates* extreme losses — exactly the failure the
[uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter exploits when Gaussian Monte-Carlo
produces tails that are too thin, and that
[gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) fixes by learning the true shape.
:::

---

## What the Labs Reload From Here

The uncertainty labs don't predict the *return* — its mean is essentially
unpredictable.  They predict the **noise**: tomorrow's volatility, which clusters
and so *is* forecastable.  The target they learn against is the **realised
annualised volatility** series we built in §2 — and this chapter is its single
home.  One recipe builds it; the labs reload that and go straight to modelling.

::: {#cell-fig-target-realised-vol .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R = datasets.load_returns()                       # prepared 14-name daily panel
σ = R["JPM"].rolling(21).std() * np.sqrt(252)     # σ(t) = σ_daily·√252   realised annualised vol
σ = σ.dropna()                                    # drop the 20-day warm-up NaNs

print("realised-vol target  ·  shape:", σ.shape)
print(σ.head().round(3).to_string())

hi = σ > σ.quantile(0.80)                          # high-volatility regime: σ(t) in its top fifth
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
ax.plot(σ.index, σ, color=INK, lw=0.8, label="realised vol σ(t)")
ax.fill_between(σ.index, 0, σ.max(), where=hi.to_numpy(),
                color=CRASH, alpha=0.12, label="high-volatility regime")
ax.set_ylabel("annualised σ"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("The realised-volatility target the labs reload", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```

date

2007-02-05    0.133
2007-02-06    0.127
2007-02-07    0.127
2007-02-08    0.128
```
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Lab Contract
This chapter **owns** the realised-volatility target.  The uncertainty labs —
[Tool 3 · Predictive Bands](../uncertainty/labs/lab-tool3-bands.qmd) and
[Job C · Predict From Noise](../uncertainty/labs/lab-jobC-predict-from-noise.qmd) —
**reload** this series with the one-liner above and predict it; they do **not**
re-derive volatility from scratch.  The only step left to the lab is the
modelling choice on top of the target: picking the **window length** (21 days
here, or an EWMA half-life), or forming the **regression pairs** $(x,\,\sigma(x))$
that the band model trains on.  The preprocessing stops here.
:::
